html:
The Hoysalas ruled most of what is now Karnataka from the 11th century to 1343. They are remembered less for their wars than for their temples, which carry some of the finest stone carving in India.

They began as hill chiefs of the Western Ghats, serving the Western Chalukyas. King Vishnuvardhana, who ruled from about 1108 to 1152, beat the Cholas at Talakad in 1116 and built the Chennakesava temple at Belur to mark it. His grandson Veera Ballala II made the kingdom fully independent about 1190. The capital moved from Belur to Halebidu, then called Dwarasamudra.

The temples are small and low, set on star-shaped platforms. They are cut from soapstone, which is soft when quarried and hardens in the air, so that carvers could work it like wood. Bands of elephants, horsemen, dancers and scenes from the epics run round every wall. The best are at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, and many sculptors signed their work. The three sites joined the World Heritage list in 2023.

Kannada poetry flourished at the court, and the teacher Ramanuja found shelter there.

Armies of the Delhi Sultanate sacked Halebidu in 1311 and again in 1327. The last king, Veera Ballala III, died fighting the sultan of Madurai in 1343. Vijayanagara took over his lands.
sum: The Hoysalas ruled most of what is now Karnataka from the 11th century to 1343. They are remembered less for their wars than for their temples, which carry some of the finest stone carving in India.
